title: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: a very large part of the specific morphology of the organism depends upon the fact that there is not only an average, or aggregate, rate of growth common to the whole, but also a variation of rate in different parts of the organism, tending towards a specific rate characteristic of each different part or organ.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Form as a function of growth rates”. Scope: multicellular organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-19: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Heterochrony and organ-specific growth are measurable in model organisms, with public developmental atlases supporting restricted tests. The broad causal contribution to multicellular morphology is too vague and taxonomically expansive for full resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate organ-specific growth trajectories and test whether their relative rates predict species- or genotype-specific adult morphology. Perturbations or natural variants that change local rates and produce the predicted form differences would support causality; unchanged morphology would refute it in that system.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Comparable trajectories across taxa are sparse.

Specific morphology and large part lack quantitative thresholds.

Local growth can be consequence as well as cause of patterning.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Organ growth curves exist in the literature and can show that local rates differ, which is the easier half of the claim. Public compilations are still mostly whole-body, and the assertion that a large part of species-specific form depends on those local rates has no sharp failure threshold. Sensitivity of shape to small rate changes is partly a mathematical property of exponential growth, so it does not by itself discriminate this account from rivals. The test stays partial.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate a specific growth rate for the whole body and for separate organs, then ask how much adult shape difference those local rate differences produce. The claim is favored if small, persistent rate differences account for a large share of between-species form; it is hard to refute, because no share is named as too small.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Organ-specific growth rates are published piecemeal.

A very large part of specific morphology does not state how large a part would fail the claim.
